name: Cooling eye mask

lead: A cooling eye mask is a gel pad or packet chilled in a fridge or freezer and placed over the closed eyes. People use it in the morning to reduce temporary puffiness around the eyes and look more awake.

Cold causes vasoconstriction and slows fluid buildup, so eyelids look less swollen after several minutes, and gentle pressure from the pad may help. Guidance from eye-care and consumer health sources supports cold compresses for transient swelling; no peer-reviewed trial of these masks was found. The effect is short-lived and cosmetic.

paras: People keep the mask in the fridge or freezer and lie back with it over closed eyes for around ten minutes after waking, often before skincare or makeup. Many use it a few mornings a week or after a short night.

Applying ice directly to eyelids can injure skin, so a barrier and short use are advised. Persistent, one-sided, painful, or vision-affecting swelling is advised to be medically reviewed, as it may indicate infection or other disease. The mask is not reported to change eye bags that are structural or fat-related.

web.title: Cold therapy and eyelid swelling (Europe PMC search)

angle.text: Users chill a gel mask and rest it over closed eyes in the morning to cut puffiness around the eyes for the next few hours. Cold narrows surface vessels and slows fluid buildup, a principle widely used for short-term swelling.

lead: A cooling eye mask is a gel pad, gel-filled packet or foam pack that is chilled in a refrigerator or freezer and placed over the closed eyes. People use it mostly in the morning to make puffy eyelids and under-eye bags look flatter, a quick way to look more rested before heading out. The change it aims for is temporary, and it takes about ten minutes.

Wikipedia's article on periorbital puffiness describes a cold compress as the main short-term remedy, noting that cold narrows blood vessels and can reduce fluid leaking into the tissue, and that raising the head during sleep is the main preventive measure mentioned [1]. Morning swelling is often most noticeable right after waking, which the article links to fluid shifting while lying flat [1].

Commercial designs include reusable gel packs in a shell or fabric, shaped masks with elastic straps, and a 2011 patent for an evaporative-cooling eye pack made from foam impregnated with polyvinyl alcohol solution [2]. No published trial has tested consumer cooling eye masks for puffy eyes, but cooling has been studied for eyelid swelling after surgery [3].

paras: Common designs are reusable gel packs in a fabric or plastic shell, sometimes shaped to fit the orbit and held with an elastic strap, and gel sheets or patches chilled before use. A 2011 patent describes an eye pack for evaporative cooling of the face near the eyes, made of a gelatinous foam impregnated with an aqueous polyvinyl alcohol solution, with a barrier on one side that lets heat pass but restricts transfer of the solution [2]. A patent shows commercial design interest and is not evidence of effect.

Wikipedia explains that periorbital puffiness is almost always from fluid buildup and that a cold pack near the eye narrows blood vessels, which can reduce fluid leaking into the tissue [1]. Gentle pressure from the pad is also said by users to help.

The same article distinguishes temporary fluid from aging changes: the fat pad under the lower eyelids enlarges over time, usually permanently [1], so structural bags are not the target of a chilled pad.

Wikipedia lists allergies as the most common cause of periorbital puffiness, along with aging, sleep posture, crying, fluid retention, diet and lifestyle factors, hypothyroidism, infections and kidney conditions [1]. It says puffy eyes are usually a temporary cosmetic concern but that severe or persistent swelling may signal a medical condition, and that swelling with fever or pain warrants evaluation [1].

Consumer eye-care guidance commonly advises placing a cloth between ice and the eyelids and keeping applications short, because very cold surfaces can injure skin. Swelling that persists, affects one side, is painful or involves vision changes is generally regarded by clinicians as needing medical assessment [1].

No studies found on consumer cooling eye masks for morning puffiness. A 2025 pilot study in 23 patients used 3D imaging to compare Hilotherapy, a controlled-cooling treatment, with untreated eyes after blepharoplasty, with one eye treated and the other as control; swelling was lower on the treated side immediately and at 24 hours [3]. This concerns post-surgical swelling, not everyday puffiness.

Cooling masks are discussed as a quick, inexpensive morning step for puffy eyes alongside sleep position, sleep duration and skincare routines. Prices are commonly quoted at about $10 to $25. Because the effect is temporary, it differs from treatments aimed at longer-term under-eye structure.

timeline.event: A patent filing describes a polyvinyl alcohol foam eye pack for evaporative cooling around the eyes. [2]
